questions.q: What does a reliability NFR primarily describe?
options: How consistently a system behaves correctly over time, including how it handles failure conditions, not just the happy path
How visually appealing the user interface is
How quickly a page loads under normal conditions
How many licensed users an org can support
questions.explain: Reliability is about correct, consistent behavior over time, specifically including what happens when something fails — a timeout, a transient error, a race condition — not just whether things work when nothing goes wrong.

questions.q: A Salesforce org is reachable 100% of the time but occasionally processes duplicate records due to a race condition. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: That the system is both highly available and highly reliable
That the system has a security NFR failure, not a reliability issue
That availability and reliability are the same thing, so this scenario is a contradiction
That the system is highly available but unreliable — availability and reliability are distinct properties
questions.explain: Availability measures whether the system is up and reachable. Reliability measures whether it behaves correctly while up. A system can be fully available yet still unreliable if it intermittently misbehaves, as with the duplicate-record scenario described.

questions.q: What does idempotency mean in the context of a Salesforce integration?
options: That an operation can only ever be performed once, with no retries allowed
That performing the same operation more than once produces the same result as performing it once
That an operation always completes within the governor-limit CPU-time budget
That an integration never needs error handling because failures can't occur
questions.explain: Idempotency means repeated execution of the same operation yields the same end state as a single execution — critical for integrations, since network failures guarantee that operations will sometimes be retried.

questions.q: Why is idempotency especially important when consuming Platform Events or Streaming API messages?
options: Because these mechanisms guarantee exactly-once delivery, so idempotency is unnecessary
Because Platform Events cannot carry an External ID field

Because these mechanisms can offer at-least-once delivery semantics, meaning a subscriber may occasionally receive the same event more than once and must handle that without creating duplicates or corrupting data
Because Streaming API only supports synchronous processing
questions.explain: At-least-once delivery semantics mean a message might be delivered more than once. A subscriber that isn't designed to tolerate duplicate delivery — through idempotent processing — risks creating duplicate records or taking an action twice.

questions.q: What does setting `allOrNone` to false on a Database DML method change about a bulk operation's reliability behavior?
options: It allows the records that succeeded to be saved while the records that failed are reported individually, rather than rolling back the entire batch over one bad record
It causes the entire batch to fail and roll back if even one record fails
It disables all governor limits for that transaction
It automatically retries failed records up to three times
questions.explain: With allOrNone set to false, a bulk DML operation saves the records that succeed and returns per-record results so failures can be identified and handled individually, instead of the default all-or-nothing rollback behavior.
